fields.supportingExcerpt: Short pieces of DNA floating in the blood, shed by dying cells all over the body. Most is from normal cells; the small tumour-derived fraction (ctDNA) is what liquid biopsies fish out.

fields.supportingExcerpt: A tube of blood contains nanograms of cell-free DNA, of which tumour DNA may be 0.01-10%. Assays detect it by deep sequencing with error correction (Guardant360, FoundationOne Liquid, MSK-ACCESS), by tumour-informed panels built from the patient's own tumour mutations (Signatera, RaDaR), or by methylation and fragment-size patterns that also reveal the tissue of origin (Galleri, fragmentomics). Uses span genotyping when tissue is scarce, resistance monitoring, MRD after surgery and multi-cancer screening. Pitfalls are CHIP-derived variants, low shedding by some tumours (brain, kidney) and pre-analytic handling, hence dedicated collection tubes.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Source classes: cfDNA is DNA outside intact cells in a sample, and ctDNA is the tumour-derived part of that pool, so the two are related materials and not rival tests. In healthy donors a methylation atlas of 25 tissues and cell types attributed plasma cfDNA to white blood cells (55%), erythrocyte progenitors (30%), vascular endothelial cells (10%) and hepatocytes (1%) (Moss 2018). A tumour adds DNA only when it contributes, and the tumour share may be small or absent in the sample drawn even when cancer exists elsewhere.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Scale: plasma DNA fragments show a pattern reminiscent of nuclease-cleaved nucleosomes with a peak at 166 base pairs (Lo 2010, in maternal plasma), and tumour-derived fragments are enriched at 90 to 150 base pairs (Mouliere 2018). One assay input in a breast-cancer comparison was 4,500 amplifiable copies, about 15 nanograms (Santonja 2023), and at about 3.3 picograms per haploid genome copy 1 nanogram is roughly 300 copies (arithmetic from genome size). In a fictional single-locus model with 4,500 amplifiable opportunities and target-allele probability 1 in 100,000, the expected target count is 0.045. The target-allele probability is not automatically a tumour-DNA fraction: copy number, variant multiplicity and clone representation matter.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Yield is not origin: in a fictional experiment equal 1 mL plasma aliquots give 2 and 4 nanograms of cfDNA and no tumour-attributed signal is reported. Total DNA doubled, but tumour fraction and any tumour-DNA fold change cannot be calculated because tumour attribution was not measured. A fragment's source needs evidence such as paired white-blood-cell and tumour sequencing (Razavi 2019), and a variant seen in plasma is not automatically tumour-derived.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Method card: measures selected features of plasma DNA by a stated sequencing or molecular method, from a finite plasma aliquot that testing consumes. Output is detected or not detected, variant fractions, molecule concentrations or model estimates, each with its own unit. It cannot give an all-body cell count, lesion location, viability or treatment benefit, and validity belongs to the exact specimen, assay version and intended use.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Collection conditions can change the mixture before testing: blood-cell breakdown adds genomic DNA and can dilute a tumour fraction. The NCI biospecimen practices document, revised February 2025, prefers plasma to serum. Its protocol recommends EDTA, accepts acid citrate dextrose, and advises avoiding heparin and citrate; the literature-summary section separately reports results with several anticoagulants when processing was immediate. For EDTA blood the protocol prefers centrifugation within 2 hours and accepts up to 4 hours at room temperature or 24 hours at 4 degrees Celsius; it recommends stabilising tubes for anticipated delays over 2 hours. These are recommendations for that specimen workflow, not a universal acceptance rule for every assay. Extraction and library preparation then retain only some available molecules, so the volume drawn is not the volume evaluated.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) consists of fragments of DNA shed by tumour cells into the blood, detectable with sensitive sequencing.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is made up of DNA fragments shed by tumour cells into the bloodstream, where they form only a small fraction of all cell-free DNA and are detected with sensitive sequencing. Its uses span genotyping for companion diagnostics, tracking resistance mutations such as EGFR T790M and ESR1, molecular residual disease, early detection and response monitoring. Shedding varies with tumour type and burden, and clonal haematopoiesis can confound results. The term underpins the Liquid biopsy (ctDNA), MRD / molecular residual disease testing and Multi-cancer early detection (MCED) technologies, and it appears in the SERENA-6, CIRCULATE-Japan and IMvigor011 trials and in ideas on molecular-progression switching beyond ESR1 and HPV ctDNA to guide cervical cancer therapy.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Detection depends on stage and tumour type: with digital PCR-based methods in 640 patients, ctDNA was found in more than 75% of people with advanced pancreatic, ovarian, colorectal, bladder, gastro-oesophageal, breast, melanoma, hepatocellular and head and neck cancers, and in fewer than 50% of primary brain, renal, prostate or thyroid cancers. In localised disease it was found in 73% of colorectal, 57% of gastro-oesophageal, 48% of pancreatic and 50% of breast adenocarcinomas, and it was often present in people with no detectable circulating tumour cells (Bettegowda 2014). The assay, specimen and population are part of each figure.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: ctDNA is a subset of cell-free DNA, and not every plasma variant is tumour-derived: in paired plasma and white-blood-cell sequencing, 53.2% of cfDNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 people without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis (Razavi 2019). A ctDNA result is also a quantity with a unit (molecules per millilitre, a fraction, or a call), and the same number means different things under each.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Lung cancer: plasma genotyping at diagnosis is non-inferior to tissue for finding a guideline biomarker (27.3% against 21.3% in 282 patients), has 100% positive predictive value for the alterations with approved drugs, returns in 9 days against 15, and raises detection by 48% when added to tissue (Leighl 2019). Clinical sensitivity against tissue is 80%, so a negative plasma result rules nothing out and the guideline permits plasma to rule in only (Lindeman 2018). Serial plasma after starting treatment also separates the patients whose resistant clone was already present, within three weeks (Oxnard 2018).

fields.supportingExcerpt: The tumour fraction estimates how much of the DNA in a plasma sample came from the tumour. A low or undetectable fraction limits what a negative test can exclude; performance thresholds belong to the particular assay and setting.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: The number that decides whether a plasma genomic result can be believed. In 45 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer whose plasma was taken on the day of a metastatic tissue biopsy, 75.6% of samples had a circulating tumour DNA proportion above 2% of total cell-free DNA; in those samples, every somatic mutation found in the matched tissue was also present in plasma, the ranking of variant allele fractions was closely similar, and copy-number calls in actionable genes agreed 88.9% of the time (Wyatt 2017). At scale, 3,129 of 3,334 men with advanced prostate cancer, 94%, had detectable circulating tumour DNA at a median tumour fraction of 7.5%, and 67 of the 72 BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations found in tissue were also found in plasma, 93%, including 100% of the variants predicted to be germline (Tukachinsky 2021). Two things confound the reading. Tumour fraction tracks disease burden, so plasma performs worst in the low-volume disease where an early answer would help most. And clonal haematopoiesis contributes variants that look somatic: at a 2% threshold, 13 of 69 men had such variants, and 7, 10%, had one in a gene used to decide PARP inhibitor candidacy, most often ATM, with clonal haematopoiesis accounting for almost half of all somatic repair-gene variants detected (Jensen 2021).
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Reading the number: a tumour fraction is an estimated share of evaluated DNA attributable to tumour, and it is a model output that depends on the method and its calibration. It is not automatically any single variant's allele fraction, and it is not a concentration such as mean tumour molecules per millilitre of plasma. Parts per million rescales a fraction only when the same quantity is meant, so a variant allele fraction of 0.01% is 100 parts per million of variant alleles and not a tumour fraction of 100 parts per million.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Fraction against concentration, fictional: two equal 1 mL aliquots each hold 4 tumour-attributed molecules. With 16 background molecules the toy share is 4 of 20, 20%. With 36 it is 4 of 40, 10%. The concentration stayed at 4 per mL while the fraction halved, so a falling fraction can come from added background DNA and not from fewer tumour molecules.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Some blood-forming cells acquire mutations and form an expanding clone. This can affect blood tests for tumour DNA and is distinct from a diagnosis of leukaemia.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP, a defined category within blood-cell clonal expansion; see the source-specific variant-fraction and clinical criteria below) is present in >10% of people over 70. It confers ~0.5-1%/year progression to myeloid neoplasm, doubles cardiovascular risk via inflammasome-primed macrophages, and predicts therapy-related MDS/AML after PARP inhibitors, platinum, and radioligand therapy. For liquid biopsy, CHIP variants are the main source of false-positive ctDNA calls, so tumour-informed or paired white-cell sequencing is needed. Interventions are preventive (avoid unnecessary genotoxic exposure, monitor) with IL-1β/IL-6 blockade under study.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Leading programmes: Ebert (Dana-Farber/Broad) and Jaiswal (Stanford) who defined CHIP; Levine and Bolton (MSK) on therapy-related clonal haematopoiesis.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Clonal haematopoiesis (CH) is the broader phenomenon of blood-cell clones carrying acquired changes. In the 2022 WHO myeloid classification, CHIP requires a somatic mutation in a myeloid-malignancy-associated gene at a variant allele fraction of at least 2%, or at least 4% for X-linked gene mutations in males, without a diagnosed haematological disorder or unexplained cytopenia (Khoury 2022). Persistent unexplained cytopenia changes the classification question. These are criteria for a named category, not a rule that every smaller blood-cell clone is absent, tumour-derived or a sequencing error.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Which genes: in blood-cell exomes from 17,182 people most clonal variants fell in DNMT3A, TET2 and ASXL1, were rare before age 40, and were seen in 9.5% of people aged 70 to 79 (Jaiswal 2014). ASXL1 mutations were enriched in current or former smokers, and radiation, platinum and topoisomerase II inhibitors selected for DNA-damage-response genes (TP53, PPM1D, CHEK2), with sequential samples showing those clones outgrowing others after exposure (Bolton 2020). In 8,810 people with non-haematological cancers, PPM1D and TP53 mutations were associated with prior chemotherapy, and clonal haematopoiesis was found in 25% (Coombs 2017).
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Source attribution in plasma, interpretation rule: TP53 is a tumour gene and also a therapy-selected blood-cell gene, so a TP53 variant in plasma after chemotherapy can come from either compartment. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess its origin; some variants remain ambiguous. In Razavi's paired sequencing 53.2% of cfDNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 controls without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis, and variants that could not be separated from white-blood-cell DNA kept an explicit ambiguous category, so subtracting every blood match is not a complete attribution method.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Fictional example: a plasma assay detects a variant that sensitive matched blood-cell sequencing finds at 0.8% VAF. The blood result supports a blood-cell contribution even below the 2% cut-off, but it does not make the variant CHIP or exclude a tumour contribution, because tumour evidence, shared variants and each method's limits still apply. Matched sequencing has its own gene coverage, depth and detection rules, so a clone below its sensitivity can stay unseen, and a clone finding is not a leukaemia diagnosis or a solid-tumour treatment instruction.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Reading the figures: a variant allele fraction counts variant alleles among the alleles evaluated and is not automatically the percentage of cells. Acquired (somatic) means not inherited and does not mean malignant. There is no age at which a plasma variant can simply be dismissed. Sequential samples show clones with DNA-damage-response mutations outgrowing others after radiation, platinum or topoisomerase II inhibitor exposure (Bolton 2020), which is selection of clones that can already be present and does not mean every new detection was caused by treatment.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Prostate cancer: this is where clonal haematopoiesis does concrete harm. In 69 men with advanced prostate cancer, clonal haematopoiesis variants at 2% or more were present in plasma from 13, 19%, and 7, 10%, had one in a gene used to decide PARP inhibitor candidacy, most often ATM, accounting for almost half of all somatic DNA repair variants detected. A paired whole-blood control distinguishes them (Jensen 2021).
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Fishing whole cancer cells out of a blood sample to count them or study them; the count is prognostic in breast, prostate and colorectal cancer.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Circulating tumour cells (CTCs) are rare cells shed by tumours into blood, roughly one per billion blood cells. The CellSearch system, cleared by the FDA in 2004, enriches them by EpCAM antibody capture and counts them; higher counts predict shorter survival in metastatic breast, prostate and colorectal cancer. Microfluidic and size-based methods capture EpCAM-negative cells, and single CTC sequencing and culture are used in research; CTC counts have not yet changed treatment in randomised trials.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: A count is a recovery under rules: enrichment concentrates candidate cells before identification, and each method selects. One established epithelial method captures with EpCAM, then checks cell shape, a nucleus, cytokeratin and absence of CD45, which is one operational definition and not a universal rule for all circulating tumour cells or tumour types. Physical methods select by size or deformability and remove or retain different cells, so marker independence is not unbiased recovery. A negative capture, such as zero qualifying cells in 7.5 mL, does not show that no tumour cells circulate and does not predict a ctDNA result, because free DNA fragments are a separate analyte.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Scale and scope: in the CellSearch system, 1 of 344 healthy or non-malignant-disease subjects (0.3%) had two or more cells per 7.5 mL, against 36% of 2,183 samples from 964 people with metastatic carcinoma, with detection of two or more cells in 57% of prostate, 37% of breast, 30% of colorectal and 20% of lung cancer samples (Allard 2004). Spiked-cell recovery averaged at least 85% over 5 to 1,142 cells. These describe that device and population.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Prognosis is not utility: in a prospective study of 177 people with metastatic breast cancer, a baseline count of 5 or more per 7.5 mL in the training set went with a median progression-free survival of 2.7 months against 7.0 (Cristofanilli 2004). In SWOG S0500, of 595 evaluable patients 123 with persistently raised counts were randomised to continue or change chemotherapy, and median overall survival was 10.7 and 12.5 months (P = .98), so that early-switch strategy did not extend survival (Smerage 2014). That bounds one strategy and neither validates nor excludes other uses of the count.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) describes changes in cell state and marker expression. Yu and colleagues reported epithelial and mesenchymal changes in circulating breast tumour cells and associations with progression (2013). As a measurement inference, enrichment requiring an epithelial marker can under-represent cells with little of that marker; physical capture has different selection effects. Neither route is a census of all circulating tumour cells. The study does not establish one marker profile for every patient or every time point.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: This blood test counts cells meeting its tumour-cell identification rules. The count has defined prognostic uses; whether changing treatment from it helps needs evidence for the particular strategy.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt:
What it measures. CellSearch pulls circulating tumour cells out of 7.5 millilitres of blood with magnetic beads coated in an antibody to EpCAM, stains them for cytokeratin and a nuclear dye, excludes white cells with CD45, and counts the cells that pass. In metastatic breast cancer five or more cells, and in metastatic prostate and colorectal cancer five or three, mark an unfavourable group.

Evidence. The 2004 New England Journal of Medicine study in metastatic breast cancer showed that women with five or more cells before starting a new treatment had far shorter progression-free and overall survival, and the FDA cleared the system the same year, then for prostate and colorectal cancer in 2008. The count also tracks response: a fall below the threshold after one cycle is a good sign. The disappointment was SWOG S0500, which switched chemotherapy early in women whose count stayed high and found no survival gain, so the count is prognostic rather than a guide to which drug to use. In hormone receptor positive breast cancer the French STIC CTC trial used the count to choose between endocrine therapy and chemotherapy and found the strategy non-inferior to the physician's choice.

Who should have it and what changes. Guidelines do not recommend routine CellSearch counts because no decision has been shown to improve outcomes from them, so use is mainly in trials and in centres studying circulating cells, where the captured cells can also be stained for HER2, androgen receptor variants or PD-L1. The test is available through Menarini Silicon Biosystems and reference laboratories at a cost similar to a specialised blood test. Circulating tumour DNA has taken over most of the clinical questions the count was meant to answer.

fields.supportingExcerpt: The cut-off belongs to its setting: 5 or more cells per 7.5 mL was the prognostic split in the 2004 metastatic breast-cancer study of 177 people, where in the training set baseline counts at or above it went with a median progression-free survival of 2.7 months against 7.0 (Cristofanilli 2004). It is not the minimum definition of a circulating tumour cell and not a universal decision threshold. A zero is a count of cells recovered and classified in one finite draw, not proof that no tumour cell circulates.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Counts have not guided treatment in the randomised test: SWOG S0500 randomised 123 of 595 evaluable patients with persistently raised counts to continue or change chemotherapy, and median overall survival was 10.7 and 12.5 months (P = .98) (Smerage 2014). Median overall survival was 35, 23 and 13 months for the groups never raised, raised then cleared, and persistently raised, which shows the count is prognostic and does not show that acting on it helps.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Historical US regulatory scope: the September 29, 2004 corrective letter for K031588 specifies enumeration of epithelial circulating tumour cells that are CD45-negative, EpCAM-positive and cytokeratin 8, 18 and/or 19-positive in whole blood. In metastatic breast cancer, at least 5 per 7.5 mL was associated with shorter progression-free and overall survival. This was an adjunctive monitoring and prognostic indication, not a universal cell-definition threshold or evidence that choosing treatment from that count improves survival. The corrective-letter date is distinct from the initial classification decision.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: A microfluidic cassette that traps cancer cells from blood by their size and stiffness rather than a surface marker, then releases them alive for testing; the first such device cleared in the United States, for metastatic breast cancer.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt:
What it does. Blood flows through a stepped microfluidic channel whose gaps narrow to a few micrometres. Large, stiff tumour cells are held in the steps while smaller, deformable blood cells pass. Reversing the flow releases the trapped cells intact, so they can be counted, stained, cultured or sequenced. Because the capture depends on physical properties rather than EpCAM, it also holds mesenchymal-like and cluster cells that antibody systems miss.

Regulatory status and evidence. In May 2022 the FDA granted De Novo authorisation to the Parsortix PC1 system for capturing and harvesting circulating tumour cells from the blood of patients with metastatic breast cancer for later analysis; it is CE marked in Europe. The clearance covers harvesting, not any specific clinical claim, so the downstream test decides what the cells mean. ANGLE, the developer, has built assays on the harvested cells for HER2, androgen receptor variants and DNA damage response markers and offers them as a service to pharmaceutical trials.

Who should have it and what changes. Nothing changes in routine care yet: harvested cells feed research and trial biomarkers rather than approved treatment decisions. Its promise is access to live tumour cells without a biopsy, for example to test protein targets that DNA cannot show, such as HER2 or oestrogen receptor on metastatic cells, and to grow cells for functional testing. Availability is through ANGLE's laboratories and partner sites; cost is that of a specialised research assay.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Interpretation rule, from the capture principle: the cassette holds cells by size and stiffness, so a cell that is small or deformable like a blood cell can pass through, and capture independent of a surface marker is not capture independent of bias. A harvested set describes the cells this method retained and not every tumour cell in the draw, and free DNA fragments in the same blood are a separate analyte that a cell harvest does not measure. Downstream protein, RNA or DNA work on harvested cells is a further assay with its own sample needs and validation.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Instead of testing blood every three months, sampling constantly, so a relapse is caught the week it starts.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: MRD testing already detects relapse months before imaging, but sampling is episodic. Work on implantable and wearable sampling, microneedle interstitial-fluid collection, and at-home dried blood spots aims to shorten the interval, while urine and saliva ctDNA reduce the burden of venepuncture. Nothing in this class was validated for clinical use by 2026, and the question of what to do with an earlier signal is still open.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: What denser sampling changes: blood draws and scans are both intermittent, so an observed gap between a first positive sample and a later event depends on both schedules and cannot locate when the signal began. In García-Murillas 2019 plasma was taken every 3 months in the first year and every 6 months after, and detection preceded clinical relapse by a median of 10.7 months (95% CI 8.1 to 19.1) in the combined cohort of 144. A median from three-monthly draws is not comparable with one from near-continuous sampling, and a shorter interval shows earlier detection and does not show that acting on it improves survival.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Fragmentomics reads the sizes and positions of DNA fragments in blood, not the mutations. Cancer cells die messily and leave a recognisable fragmentation pattern.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Fragmentomics analyses genome-wide cell-free DNA fragment length, end motifs, and nucleosome footprints at low sequencing depth, which is cheaper than deep mutation or methylation sequencing. DELFI Diagnostics commercialised FirstLook Lung (2023) as a blood test to increase uptake of low-dose CT screening, and presented the first randomised clinical-utility data (L301 FIRSTLUNG) at ATS 2026. Fragment features are also being layered into multi-cancer detection and MRD assays by Guardant, GRAIL, and academic groups.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Measure, then infer: the measured features are fragment length, end sequences, genomic positions and chemical marks. A reference or trained model then turns them into a source estimate or a score, so the output is an inference and not a cell census, and no single fragment carries a cancer address. Tumour fragments are shorter on average, but most short fragments in a sample still come from normal cells because normal DNA outnumbers tumour DNA when the tumour fraction is low. These features can complement mutation tracking when few informative mutations are sampled, and neither a source estimate nor a score by itself establishes tumour location, stage, a resistance mechanism or benefit from acting on a result.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Evidence read: selecting fragments of 90 to 150 base pairs gave more than twofold median enrichment of tumour DNA in over 95% of cases among 344 plasma samples from 200 people with cancer (Mouliere 2018). A genome-wide fragmentation classifier detected 57% to more than 99% of seven cancer types at 98% specificity (area under the curve 0.94) in 236 patients and 245 healthy people, and located tissue of origin to a limited number of sites in 75% of cases (Cristiano 2019). Nucleosome footprints in cfDNA correlate with cell-type epigenetics (Snyder 2016). Each is a proof of principle in defined cohorts and does not transfer to another population, collection protocol or assay version.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Handling is part of the measurement: neither collection tube nor plasma processing time changed cfDNA fragment sizes in one study, but both could change genome-wide fragmentation patterns and fragment-end sequences, and a size profile that looks fine is an incomplete quality check (van der Pol 2022). In a fictional case a classifier trained on promptly processed plasma gives higher scores on samples transported under another protocol while DNA yield meets the minimum, and that does not show more cancer-associated DNA until the new conditions are validated.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Blood tests that read chemical marks on fragments of DNA shed by tumours; the marks tell cancer DNA from normal DNA and hint at where the cancer is.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Cancer cells carry characteristic DNA methylation patterns that survive in the cell-free DNA shed into blood. Methylation-based tests use bisulfite or enzymatic conversion followed by targeted sequencing to detect a cancer signal and predict its tissue of origin; the multi-cancer early detection test Galleri works this way, and Guardant's Shield, the first blood test approved by the FDA for colorectal cancer screening in 2024, combines methylation with other cfDNA signals. Methylation also underpins some minimal residual disease assays.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: How the read works: DNA methylation adds chemical marks to DNA bases without changing sequence, and many assays examine methylated cytosines next to guanines (CpG sites), using chemical or enzymatic conversion or other technologies. Normal cell types carry their own methylation patterns, so a mark is not a cancer label. Deconvolution estimates how much each reference cell type contributes to a mixture: a methylation atlas of 25 tissues and cell types attributed healthy-donor plasma cfDNA to white blood cells (55%), erythrocyte progenitors (30%), vascular endothelial cells (10%) and hepatocytes (1%), and its contributions also matched sepsis and islet transplantation (Moss 2018).
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Scope: a classifier assigns a score or category and a deconvolution assigns source fractions, and both depend on the reference set, the model and the cut-off. Because tissue injury also adds normal DNA from an organ, an inferred organ contribution alone is not proof of cancer. A model validated in one population, collection protocol and assay version does not transfer automatically, and a score is not necessarily a calibrated probability.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Residual disease testing looks for small amounts of disease after treatment using a specified sample and method. A negative result means no qualifying signal was detected under that test, rather than proof that no cancer remains.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Minimal, measurable and molecular residual disease (MRD) are related terms for small amounts of disease assessed after treatment with a specified method and specimen. A negative result means no qualifying signal was detected under that method, not proof that every cancer cell is absent. In leukaemia and myeloma it is measured by flow cytometry or NGS of marrow (clonoSEQ); in solid tumours it means ctDNA after surgery, covered under MRD / molecular residual disease testing. MRD positivity predicts relapse, MRD-guided escalation (IMvigor011) and de-escalation (DYNAMIC) are proven concepts, and MRD is an accepted endpoint in myeloma trials (FDA ODAC 2024). Readers meet it in the Colorectal, Pancreatic, Bladder & urothelial, DLBCL and Multiple myeloma entries and in CIRCULATE-Japan.
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: The name has three expansions: minimal residual disease (small remaining amounts), measurable residual disease (used in blood-cancer guidance, stressing what the method can detect) and molecular residual disease (tumour-associated molecular signals after treatment, mostly ctDNA in solid tumours). Check which one a paper means. Cell-frequency thresholds in leukaemia, molecular ratios and plasma detection rules are different quantities, and the European LeukemiaNet update on acute myeloid leukaemia sets disease-specific techniques, materials, time points and thresholds that are not transferable to a solid tumour (Heuser 2021).

Twenty independent loci with the same opportunity count and probability give an expected total of 9 and exp(-9), 0.012%, for none. Independence, equal recovery and one retained target being sufficient are assumptions of this model. These are not measured clinical false-negative rates. A tumour-DNA fraction cannot simply replace the target-allele probability without assumptions about copy number, variant multiplicity and which tumour clones carry the variant. More reads cannot recover an original molecule absent from the aliquot.

Trials so far have used tumour-informed tests for treatment decisions (DYNAMIC used a tumour-informed approach; IMvigor011 used Signatera), while screening tests are necessarily tumour-naive. Head-to-head sensitivity comparisons are few, and results are not interchangeable between assays.

fields.supportingExcerpt:
Lead time is the interval between the moment a screening test finds a cancer and the moment that cancer would have been diagnosed because it caused symptoms. Lead-time bias is what happens when survival is measured from diagnosis: a man whose cancer is found five years earlier appears to survive five years longer even if the date of his death is unchanged. It is why survival from diagnosis is unreliable on its own as a measure of whether a screening programme works, and why randomised screening trials report mortality in the whole invited population instead.

For prostate-specific antigen screening, estimated lead time depends on the definition and population. The following numbers are model estimates from specified settings, not a ranking of lead times across cancers. Draisma and Etzioni ran three independently built models of prostate cancer progression and detection, all calibrated to Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results incidence in United States men aged 54 to 80 between 1985 and 2000. Among screen-detected cancers that would have surfaced in the man's lifetime, mean lead time was 5.4 to 6.9 years across the three models; the original MISCAN model fitted instead to the Rotterdam section of the European screening trial gave 7.9 years. Published estimates before that work spanned 3 to 12 years. The three models agreed closely with each other for any single definition of lead time and disagreed substantially across definitions, which is the paper's real finding: the number is a property of the question, not of the disease.

The consequence is practical. Lead time is what generates overdiagnosis: if the lead time is longer than the man's remaining life, the cancer would never have troubled him, and the same modelling put overdiagnosis at 23 to 42 percent of screen-detected cancers in the United States calibration and 66 percent in the Rotterdam one. It is also why the 2018 United States task force statement expresses benefit as deaths and metastatic cases prevented per 1,000 men screened over about 13 years rather than as a survival rate, and why the two 2009 randomised trials, ERSPC and PLCO, are the evidence rather than any registry series.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Why a five-year survival rate cannot settle a screening argument. Three biases push it up without anyone living longer: lead-time bias, because the clock starts earlier; length bias, because a test that samples the population at intervals preferentially catches slow-growing cancers that sit around waiting to be found; and overdiagnosis, because cancers that would never have surfaced are added to the numerator of survivors. All three run in the same direction. Mortality in a randomised invited population is immune to all three, which is why it is the endpoint the trials used.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Lead time is not the same as overdiagnosis, although the two are produced by the same mechanism. Lead time is how much earlier the diagnosis came. Overdiagnosis is the case where the lead time exceeded the rest of the man's life, so the diagnosis never needed to come at all. A long lead time with a long life left is exactly what screening is for.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Lead time is the interval between defined earlier and later detection events. Lead-time bias occurs when that timing difference is mistaken for a better outcome. In a fictional course, detection at year 4 and death at year 6 gives two years from diagnosis. Moving detection to year 3 with death still at year 6 gives three recorded years without adding life. Similarly, labelling post-treatment recurrence at a blood signal before imaging confirmation can mechanically lengthen survival measured from recurrence. Align the endpoint, qualifying event and clock origin. Ten months of detection lead time is not ten added months of life. Earlier effective intervention could help, but its benefit needs separate evidence; correcting the clock alone does not solve selection, confounding or missing follow-up.

Comparing that strategy with a meaningful alternative from a common origin, such as randomisation, can assess clinical outcomes and harms. Analysis must also address when groups entered, how follow-up ended, whether positive tests triggered extra imaging and whether people without prior detection were omitted. c-TRAK TN tested a specific blood-surveillance and intervention design; its detection and feasibility findings do not establish a beneficial intervention window for every early signal. A fictional contrast of median survival of 24 months after blood detection versus 18 after imaging detection, without a common-origin comparison, cannot show that testing saves lives. Some or all of the difference could arise from the earlier clock or other group differences.

fields.supportingExcerpt: The same timing distinction extends beyond the prostate-screening context of this record. Historical breast-cancer surveillance trials illustrate why strategy and outcome must stay together. Rosselli Del Turco and colleagues' 1994 trial enrolled 1,243 surgically treated patients with unilateral invasive breast cancer and no metastases. Adding six-monthly chest radiographs and bone scans detected more isolated intrathoracic and bone metastases, 112 versus 71, and the report described earlier detection of recurrences in that group; five-year relapse-free survival, which stops at detection, was significantly lower with intensive follow-up, while five-year mortality was 18.6% versus 19.5%, with no mortality improvement reported. The separate GIVIO trial enrolled 1,320 women and reported no overall-survival or quality-of-life difference, and no significant difference in time to recurrence detection. Thus the trials should not both be described as showing earlier detection: only the first reported it. Their results do not establish equivalence or the effects of modern imaging and treatment, and a nonsignificant comparison is not proof of exactly zero benefit.

Because draws and scans are both intermittent, the gap begins at an observed draw and cannot locate biological onset, and an earlier signal shows earlier detection and not longer survival, which is the lead-time bias problem.

fields.supportingExcerpt:
Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) can be reported as a concentration, as a fraction, or as a yes or no call, and the three are not interchangeable. A concentration counts tumour-attributed molecules in a stated volume of plasma. One example is mean tumour molecules per millilitre (MTM/mL), which the I-SPY 2 breast-cancer study of Magbanua and colleagues used for ctDNA across tracked variants. A fraction divides tumour-attributed molecules by a stated total, such as all evaluated alleles at one position (variant allele fraction, VAF) or all evaluated DNA (an estimated tumour fraction). Parts per million (PPM) is a fraction multiplied by one million, so the number is only as meaningful as the fraction it scales: 0.01% is 100 PPM, and 0.00024% is 2.4 PPM, the lowest allele fraction Santonja and colleagues reported for ctDNA detection in breast cancer.

Concentration and fraction can move apart. If two equal one-millilitre aliquots each hold the same number of tumour molecules but one holds more background cell-free DNA, the concentration is unchanged and the fraction falls. A detection call and a reliable amount are also different claims, because the detection limit and the quantitation range are validated separately. Nothing here gives a conversion between assays: MTM/mL cannot be turned into PPM from the printed result, and a VAF of 100 PPM at one variant is not a tumour fraction of 100 PPM.

fields.supportingExcerpt:
A circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) assay looks for tumour-associated features in a finite sample of cell-free DNA. How much tumour DNA reaches the sampled blood varies between lesions, and recovery, background DNA, the features tracked and the assay's detection limit all shape the call. Imaging measures a defined region through a physical signal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast can report contrast enhancement or the volume of enhancing tissue, which is not a direct count of viable cancer cells. The two tests can therefore differ without either being wrong, and neither automatically replaces the other.

They can also share information. In Magbanua and colleagues' pilot of 84 women having neoadjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer, ctDNA concentration was correlated with MRI functional tumour volume at all four time points, with Spearman correlations of 0.42 to 0.49, and patients with detectable ctDNA had a higher median volume. Agreement was partial, and adding ctDNA early in treatment to volume-based prediction of pathological complete response gave only a numerical gain that was not statistically significant. ctDNA positivity after treatment added significantly to volume for predicting distant recurrence and death. A mismatch calls for checking dates, assay limits, the imaged region and the exact finding. It does not by itself show a false test or hidden metastatic disease.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Lead time is the measured gap between a first qualifying positive blood sample and a later clinical event. It depends on who is counted and when tests were done, and it is not extra life.

fields.supportingExcerpt:
In a ctDNA monitoring study, lead time is the date of a defined later event, such as confirmed clinical recurrence, minus the date of the first qualifying positive blood sample. The definition needs rules: whether recurrence means imaging, pathology or symptoms, whether the blood date is collection or reporting, whether a positive result triggered an extra scan, and whether treatment began on the signal. Blood draws and scans are both intermittent, so the observed gap reflects both schedules. A negative draw at month 3 and a first positive at month 6 do not locate when the signal began.

The denominator matters as much as the number. A median taken only over people with both an earlier positive and a later recurrence describes that selected group. It leaves out recurrences with no earlier positive, and people who are positive but have not recurred at the data cutoff have unfinished intervals, which are censored rather than zero or infinite. In García-Murillas and colleagues' prospective breast-cancer study, with blood taken every 3 months in the first year and every 6 months after, ctDNA detection preceded clinical relapse by a median of 10.7 months (95% CI 8.1 to 19.1) in the combined cohort of 144, and ctDNA found distant extracranial relapse in 22 of 23 patients but brain-only relapse in 1 of 6. In the c-TRAK TN trial, ctDNA was detected in 27.3% by 12 months and 7 patients relapsed without prior detection. A longer lead time shows earlier detection. It does not show that acting on the signal helps people live longer, which is the separate lead-time bias problem.

A primary error-suppression study combined molecular barcoding and background correction to improve detection in a defined assay. Another primary comparison examined tumor-informed and tumor-naive assays on matched breast cancer samples. Their findings do not create one universal detection limit: sample input, tracked features and the complete workflow remain part of the result.

fields.supportingExcerpt: For independent random target-molecule counts with Poisson mean lambda, the chance of none is exp(-lambda). At lambda = 1 this is 36.8%, so an average of one does not guarantee a molecule. In a fictional model, an evaluated aliquot supplies 4,500 independent amplifiable opportunities at one locus, each with a target-allele probability of 1 in 10,000. The expected target count is 0.45. If target counts follow a Poisson distribution, the chance of no target is exp(-0.45), 63.8%. Twenty independent loci with the same opportunity count and probability give an expected total of 9 and exp(-9), 0.012%, for none. Independence, equal recovery and one retained target being sufficient are assumptions of this model. These are not measured clinical false-negative rates. A tumour-DNA fraction cannot simply replace the target-allele probability without assumptions about copy number, variant multiplicity and which tumour clones carry the variant. More reads cannot recover an original molecule absent from the aliquot.

fields.supportingExcerpt: A worked example: in a multiplex PCR assay with a theoretical limit of 1 / (4,500 copies x variants), one sample not detected with 4,500 amplifiable copies was detected at 7.9 parts per million when re-assayed with 27,000 copies, and the authors note that detection at the theoretical limit rests on a single mutant molecule and is subject to the stochastic nature of sampling (Santonja 2023). A nominal detection limit from high-input validation material may not apply to a low-input clinical sample, so a laboratory with a 95% detection claim at 30 units of input cannot attach the same claim to a sample with 5 units without supporting data.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Analytical detection and clinical sensitivity answer different questions. FDA diagnostic-test guidance dated March 2007 defines clinical sensitivity by the proportion testing positive among people who have the specified condition, judged against the reference standard in the intended-use population. In a residual-disease study, disease definition, follow-up, draw schedule, evaluable samples and recurrence sites shape that denominator. An analytical limit measured in prepared material does not supply that clinical proportion, and a negative test does not establish absence of cancer.

Repeated draws observe different times, but tumour biology and handling can make their errors correlated; they are not automatically independent repeats. A failed sample or an unbuildable reference needs its stated failure disposition rather than being silently called negative.

Matched blood-cell sequencing helped attribute origin. A technically real somatic variant is not necessarily tumor-derived, and origin cannot be assigned from the gene name alone. This measurement problem is distinct from assessing the future health implications of a blood-cell clone.

fields.supportingExcerpt: How common it is: in paired plasma and white-blood-cell sequencing, 53.2% of cfDNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 people without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis, and variants that could not be separated from white-blood-cell DNA kept an explicit ambiguous category (Razavi 2019). Blood-cell clones also fall into gene groups: DNMT3A, TET2 and ASXL1 with age (Jaiswal 2014) and TP53, PPM1D and CHEK2 selected by radiation, platinum and topoisomerase II inhibitors (Bolton 2020). A gene often mutated in tumours is therefore not proof of tumour origin.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Attribution rule: matched white-blood-cell sequencing is the standard comparison, but its gene coverage, depth and detection rules matter, a clone below its sensitivity can stay unseen, and subtracting every blood match is not a complete method because a variant can be present in blood and tumour. In a fictional case the same variant V is detected in plasma and blood cells and not in the sampled tumour. That supports a blood-cell contribution, and tumour non-detection is not a biological zero because it is bounded by coverage, sensitivity, timing and the region sampled.

fields.supportingExcerpt: A test may detect that a signal is present before it can measure its amount reliably. Both limits need to be defined for the method and sample conditions.

fields.supportingExcerpt: A detection limit concerns the lowest amount that can be detected under stated conditions; a quantitation limit concerns an amount measurable with suitable accuracy and precision. These are analytical properties, distinct from the proportion of patients with a condition who test positive. Input, recovery, background, calling rules and acceptable error influence what a stated limit means. The FDA/ICH source supplies general analytical definitions for drug procedures, not certification of any particular clinical tumor-DNA assay. The ICH Q2(R2) glossary, as reproduced in FDA guidance, defines the detection limit as the lowest amount of an analyte that can be detected but not necessarily quantitated as an exact value, and the quantitation limit as the lowest amount that can be quantitatively determined with suitable precision and accuracy. It defines accuracy as closeness of agreement between an accepted reference value and the measured value, and precision as the closeness of agreement, or scatter, between a series of measurements of the same homogeneous sample, which is usually expressed as a variance, standard deviation or coefficient of variation. Mass spectrometry assay validation also considers the limit of the blank, the lower limit of quantification, linearity and parallelism (Carr and colleagues, 2014).
fields.semanticStatus: Exact current-field anchor; source-to-requirement acceptance remains pending.

fields.supportingExcerpt: A detection call and a reliable amount are different claims: the limit of detection describes detection probability under specified conditions and the limit of quantitation describes where a number is reliable, and the two have separate validation criteria. A value detected below the quantitative range does not support an exact fold change. In ctDNA reporting, a concentration such as mean tumour molecules per millilitre, a fraction such as variant allele fraction and a call are different quantities, so the fictional 0.01% variant allele fraction (100 parts per million of variant alleles) cannot be compared with a 0.2 molecules per millilitre report without both assays' methods and calibration.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Detection and quantitation need different validation criteria. The terminology appendix of a November 2018 FDA technical review defines a detection limit using a specified detection probability and a quantitation limit using stated accuracy, or bias and precision, requirements. That review concerns a malaria biomarker, not an oncology-assay validation. The distinction explains why detection below a validated quantitative range does not justify an exact fold change; a commonly used 95% detection criterion is a specified convention, not a property guaranteed for every input or sample.

fields.supportingExcerpt: The original enzyme-linked immunospot method counted antibody-secreting cells; cytokine versions are used to examine stimulated immune-cell responses. Cancer Vaccine Consortium proficiency panels showed that sample handling, protocol choices and plate reading affected results. A result needs the measured molecule, stimulation, cell input, background and reporting rule. A positive secretion response alone does not show that the sampled cells recognize or kill an unmodified tumor.

fields.supportingExcerpt: Method card, what it measures: cells that secrete a chosen molecule, most often interferon gamma, under defined stimulation, counted as spots on an antibody-coated membrane. How: capture antibodies hold the released molecule near the cell, the cells are removed and detection reagents make localised spots visible. Input: viable cells, often PBMCs, allocated to the test. Prior culture expansion changes the measured population, and the cells are removed before the membrane spots are read. Output: spot-forming units per stated number of input cells, with background handling stated. Thresholds: response and quality rules fixed in advance for that assay and study, so one paper's positivity rule is not imported into another laboratory's report. Failure modes: high background, dead cells, weak stimulation, merged spots, inconsistent counting or failed controls. It cannot tell each receptor's target, natural tumour recognition, safety in healthy tissue or clinical benefit.

Background-subtracted, that is 30 minus 5 = 25 spots per 100,000 cells, or 250 spot-forming units per million input cells. This is an arithmetic summary and not a positivity cut-off, replicates, positive controls and a prespecified response rule still apply, and in mixed PBMCs it is not the frequency of a particular T-cell subset. If the cells came from an expanded culture, the number describes the cultured cells and not the responding fraction of the original blood draw.

fields.supportingExcerpt: What the evidence does and does not support: the interferon gamma ELISpot is described as measuring the difference in the number of cells secreting the molecule with and without peptide, and interferon gamma is produced predominantly by natural killer and natural killer T cells as well as Th1 CD4 and CD8 effector T cells, so a mixed-cell spot does not by itself name the responding cell (Wykes and Renia protocol). Peptide added to cells can bypass the tumour's own processing and presentation, so a peptide response needs a separate bridge to natural tumour recognition.

ELISpot asks how many input cells release the chosen molecule under the stated stimulation. An expanded sequence does not establish that it caused a spot, and a spot in mixed cells does not identify a receptor sequence. Connecting identity to recognition or killing requires additional experiments with suitable controls.

Immunophenotyping uses combinations of markers to distinguish cell populations, including in blood-cancer diagnosis and residual-disease testing. Other methods measure intracellular cytokines, degranulation or target-cell death. Primary method studies show that these are different readouts, and validation depends on preparation, panel, controls and analysis gates. The performance of one assay does not automatically validate every use of the platform.

Binding is 100 / 1,000 = 10% of the T-cell parent, 100 / 10,000 = 1% of recovered cells and 100 / 12,000 = 0.83% of recorded events. All three are correct for their own question and exchanging them changes the claim. Nested gates show membership and not area, no cells per millilitre or whole-body total follows, and binding or marker identity does not show killing.

Input: whole blood, isolated cells or dissociated tissue, where preparation and staining use a defined aliquot and compatibility with later assays depends on fixation and other processing and tissue dissociation removes geography and can recover cell types unevenly. Output: event counts, percent of a named parent population, fluorescence in instrument-dependent units, and cells per volume only with a validated counting method. Controls: instrument checks, unstained and single-stain controls, viability, biological controls and fluorescence-minus-one controls for hard boundaries. Failure modes: dead cells, aggregates, weak markers, nonspecific staining, signal overlap, cell loss and inconsistent gates. It cannot tell unmeasured proteins, original tissue position, antigen specificity from general markers or benefit.

fields.supportingExcerpt: What compensation does and does not do: in multicolour analysis spectral overlap between detectors needs compensation, and a mathematical and experimental analysis showed that photon-counting statistics add a nonlinear error to compensated parameters while measurement and log-scale binning errors add linear ones, most visibly with red and far-red fluorochromes where less light is emitted (Roederer 2001). Compensation or spectral unmixing therefore corrects overlap and does not repair a poorly chosen stain or set a positivity gate. The community guidelines (Cossarizza 2021) are methods guidance on preparation, panels and analysis and give no universal immune-response cut-off. A degranulation marker on the cell surface is an activity readout that accompanied cytolysis in antigen-specific CD8 T cells and is not itself measured target-cell death (Betts 2003).

fields.supportingExcerpt: Gating is selection within recorded data, not physical collection. A typical analysis checks acquisition quality, excludes debris and cell pairs, assesses viability where the assay requires it, and identifies populations with a stated marker panel. Intracellular assays may assess viability before fixation; not every flow experiment studies living cells. Fluorescence-minus-one controls omit one stain while retaining the others and can help place a boundary, but do not establish antibody specificity. Tight earlier gates can discard unexpected or rare populations. Automated clusters still need biological and technical checks (Cossarizza 2021). A cell sorter can physically collect selected events for downstream work, subject to recovery, purity and functional-viability requirements; an analytical gate alone does not do this (Cossarizza 2019).

Counts of recorded events, percentages of a gate and cells per original blood volume are different outputs. The 2021 community guidelines describe both bead-based and instrument-based counting in specific protocols; neither makes every marker panel a validated clinical test.

That study concerned viral responses, not cancer-treatment prediction. The stimulated material, measured cytokines, cell groups and analysis gates define the result. Cytokine production is distinct from direct measurement of target-cell death, and assay validation does not by itself establish clinical benefit.
